question_html: How should inventories be generally valued according to the principle of conservative accounting?

options.C: At lower of cost or net realizable value
options.D: At replacement cost or market price whichever is higher

answer_html: Answer: (C) Inventories are generally valued at the lower of cost or net realizable value as governed by the principle of conservative accounting[cite: 14].

question_html: Which of the following cost components is excluded from the cost of inventories?

options.A: Cost of purchase including non-refundable duties
options.B: Costs of conversion including systematic allocation of fixed overheads
options.C: Abnormal amounts of wasted materials and labour
options.D: Other costs incurred in bringing inventories to present location and condition

answer_html: Answer: (C) Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production overheads are excluded from the cost of inventories[cite: 14].

question_html: What is the effect on net income if the closing inventory is overstated?
answer_html: Answer: (B) If the closing inventory is overstated, cost of goods sold is understated, which leads to an overstatement of net income[cite: 14].

question_html: Which inventory record system determines cost of goods sold directly and takes closing inventory as a balancing figure using continuous book records?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Under the perpetual inventory system, cost of goods sold is directly determined and inventory of goods is taken as a balancing figure using an inventory ledger[cite: 14].

question_html: Which inventory valuation method is NOT permitted by Accounting Standards?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Accounting Standards do not permit the usage of the LIFO method because it relies on an irrational assumption regarding goods flow[cite: 14].

question_html: What is another name for the Adjusted Selling Price method of determining inventory cost?
answer_html: Answer: (B) The adjusted selling price method is also widely known as the retail inventory method[cite: 14].

question_html: Under the Periodic Inventory System, how is the cost of goods sold determined?

options.A: Opening Inventory + Purchases - Closing Inventory (physically counted)
options.D: Opening Inventory + Cost of Goods Manufactured

answer_html: Answer: (A) Cost of goods sold under periodic inventory system is calculated as Opening Inventory + Purchases + Direct Expenses - Closing Inventory[cite: 14].

question_html: When is the Specific Identification Method of inventory valuation generally used?

options.A: For items that are ordinary, interchangeable, and low in value
options.B: For items that are not ordinarily interchangeable and have high individual value like expensive medical equipment
options.C: For retail businesses with rapidly changing items
options.D: For raw materials like crude oil

answer_html: Answer: (B) Specific identification method is used for items not ordinarily interchangeable and of high value, such as expensive equipment[cite: 14].

question_html: What is the Net Realizable Value (NRV) generally considered to be for raw materials held for the production of finished goods?

options.C: Estimated selling price of finished goods

answer_html: Answer: (B) In the case of raw materials held for production, replacement cost is generally considered as net realizable value[cite: 14].
topic_text: Net Realizable Value for Raw Materials

question_html: Under inflationary trends, which inventory costing method will show the highest value of closing inventory?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Under FIFO, closing inventory consists of the latest and highest purchases during rising prices, showing the highest inventory value[cite: 14].
topic_text: Impact of Inflation on Inventory Methods

question_html: If the profit margin is 25% on cost price, what percentage of the selling price is the profit?
answer_html: Answer: (C) If profit is 25% (or 1/4th) of cost, it is 20% (or 1/5th) of the selling price[cite: 14].

question_html: Where are inventories disclosed in the financial statements of a company as per Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Inventories are classified and disclosed under current assets in the financial statements[cite: 14].

question_html: Which of the following is NOT included in the cost of purchase of inventory?

options.D: GST paid on purchase which is available as input tax credit

answer_html: Answer: (D) GST on purchase that is recoverable/available as credit from tax authorities is excluded from the cost of purchase[cite: 14].

question_html: What is the standard method used when there are frequent changes in the unit price of goods purchased often, such as crude oil?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Standard cost method is used when unit prices change frequently and goods like crude oil are purchased regularly[cite: 14].

question_html: What is the treatment of storage costs in inventory valuation under normal circumstances?

options.B: Excluded from inventory cost unless necessary in the production process prior to further production

answer_html: Answer: (B) Storage costs are normally excluded unless they are necessary in the production process prior to a further production stage (like wine fermentation)[cite: 14].

question_html: If the opening inventory is understated by ₹20,000, what is the impact on the net income for the accounting period?
answer_html: Answer: (B) As per the income determination rules in Chapter 4, if opening inventory is understated, cost of goods sold is understated, which results in net income being overstated[cite: 14].
topic_text: Effect of Inventory Misstatement on Income

question_html: Cost of goods sold is ₹80,700, opening inventory is ₹5,800, and closing inventory is ₹6,000. What is the amount of purchases?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Cost of Goods Sold = Opening + Purchases - Closing $\implies$ $80,700 = 5,800 + \text{Purchases} - 6,000 \implies$ Purchases = $80,700 - 5,800 + 6,000 = \text{₹}80,900$[cite: 14].

question_html: Average inventory is ₹12,000. Closing inventory is ₹3,000 more than opening inventory. What is the value of closing inventory?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Average Inventory = (Opening + Closing) / 2 = 12,000 $\implies$ Opening + Closing = 24,000. Let Opening = $x$, Closing = $x + 3,000$. Thus $x + x + 3,000 = 24,000 \implies 2x = 21,000 \implies x = 10,500$ (Opening). Closing = $10,500 + 3,000 = \text{₹}13,500$[cite: 14].

question_html: If closing inventory of the previous year was valued more by ₹50,000, how does it affect previous year's and current year's profit?

options.A: Previous year's profit is overstated and current year's profit is also overstated
options.B: Previous year's profit is overstated and current year's profit is understated
options.C: Previous year's profit is understated and current year's profit is overstated

answer_html: Answer: (B) Overstating previous year's closing inventory overstates that year's profit. Since that closing inventory becomes current year's opening inventory, it understates the current year's profit[cite: 14].
topic_text: Effect of Inventory Error Across Years

question_html: Cost of goods available for sale is ₹1,00,000, total sales is ₹80,000, opening inventory is ₹20,000, and gross profit margin on sales is 25%. What is the closing inventory for the year?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Cost of goods sold = Sales - Gross Profit = $80,000 - (25\% \text{ of } 80,000) = 80,000 - 20,000 = \text{₹}60,000$. Closing Inventory = Cost of goods available for sale - Cost of goods sold = $1,00,000 - 60,000 = \text{₹}40,000$[cite: 14].
topic_text: Closing Inventory Computation from Sales and GP

question_html: Goods purchased amount to ₹1,00,000, sales amount to ₹90,000, and margin is 20% on cost. What is the value of closing inventory (assuming opening inventory is nil)?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Cost of Goods Sold = Sales / (1 + Rate on cost) = $90,000 / 1.20 = \text{₹}75,000$. Closing Inventory = Opening (0) + Purchases (1,00,000) - COGS (75,000) = \text{₹}25,000$[cite: 14].
topic_text: Closing Inventory with Margin on Cost

question_html: Opening inventory on 1.12.2022 is 50 units valued at ₹2,200. Purchases: 2.12.2022 - 100 units @ ₹47; 4.12.2022 - issued 50 units; 5.12.2022 - purchased 200 units @ ₹48. Using weighted average method, what is the value of inventory at the end of the week and unit weighted average cost?
answer_html: Answer: (A) As per multiple choice question answers in Chapter 4, the correct value is ₹14,200 and unit weighted average cost is ₹47.33[cite: 14].

question_html: Physical verification of stock was done on 23rd June 2022 and its value was ₹48,00,000. Unsold goods on consignment were ₹2,40,000. Purchases made between 23rd June and 30th June were ₹4,00,000, out of which goods worth ₹1,60,000 were delivered on 5th July (goods in transit). Sales were ₹13,60,000 (including ₹3,20,000 sent on approval, half of which were returned before 30th June). Goods are sold at cost plus 25% (except goods costing ₹2,40,000 sold for ₹1,20,000). What is the value of stock on 30th June 2022?
answer_html: Answer: (A) As shown in Practical Question 4 of Chapter 4, the value of stock on 30th June 2022 is ₹44,64,000[cite: 14].
topic_text: Inventory Taking at a Date Other Than Year End

question_html: A trader closed books on 31st March 2022 but stock taking was done on 9th April 2022, valued at ₹2,50,000. Sales between 31st March and 9th April were ₹17,200 (gross profit 33.33% on cost). Purchases were ₹1,200, out of which goods worth ₹500 were received after stock taking. Goods invoiced in March but received on 4th April amounted to ₹1,000. What is the value of physical stock as on 31st March 2022?
answer_html: Answer: (A) As demonstrated in Practical Question 1 of Chapter 4, backing up stock from 9th April to 31st March results in ₹2,61,200[cite: 14].

question_html: Net profit as per P&L is ₹6,000,000 after closing stock of ₹3,75,000 on 31st March 2022. Scrutiny revealed: purchase of shop electric fittings ₹15,000 charged to purchases; goods given as free samples ₹40,000 unrecorded; purchase invoice ₹2,50,000 entered in March but goods omitted from stock; sales of ₹2,000,000 delivered in March taken in April sales; goods costing ₹75,000 sent on approval in March (approved in April) taken as March sales. What is the adjusted net profit?
answer_html: Answer: (A) As per Practical Question 3 solution in Chapter 4, the adjusted net profit is ₹10,40,000[cite: 14].
topic_text: Adjusted Net Profit and Stock Adjustments
